confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (0 state the same rule, 1 refine it); none contradicts.

new_statements.quote: c. Stress falls on the last syllable of the word: fa.'in ‘woman’, kin.ba.'lin ‘his/her friend’, ka.ka.'ruk ‘chicken’. d. In a word-final sequence of ui or iu the u is stressed and i is pronounced as a glide: piu ‘ground’ is pronounced [pyu] and pakanibui ‘wave’ as [pakani'buy]. (p. 10) Monosyllabic roots predominate, while stress in polysyllabic words occurs on the final syllable. (p. 4)
new_statements.citation: Rowe, Karen (2005). Siar grammar essentials. Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics.
new_statements.locator: p. 10, §2.4 'Phonotactics and stress', item (c) and (d) [PDF page 18]; also p. 4, §1.7 'Typological overview' [PDF page 12]
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: matches PROVENANCE; 126 pp., text; the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Siar Ess_final version 1st Nov05'). PDF page 18 = printed p. 10, heading '2.4 Phonotactics and stress', item (c) reads exactly: 'Stress falls on the last syllable of the word: fa.'in ‘woman’, kin.ba.'lin ‘his/her friend’, ka.ka.'ruk ‘chicken’.' and item (d): 'In a word-final sequence of ui or iu the u is stressed and i is pronounced as a glide: piu ‘ground’ is pronounced [pyu] and pakanibui ‘wave’ as [pakani'buy].' PDF page 12 = printed p. 4, §1.7 Typological overview: 'Monosyllabic roots predominate, while stress in polysyllabic words occurs on the final syllable.' All three passages verbatim as quoted. Surrounding §2.3…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog final stress is fixed final stress; Rowe states 'Stress falls on the last syllable of the word' with three examples. Same placement, same type.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is on the last syllable of the word, without exception stated; in a word-final vowel sequence ui/iu the u carries the stress and the i is a glide, so the final syllable is still the stressed one.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The only refinement is the glide rule for final ui/iu sequences (u stressed, i a glide), which keeps stress final.
new_statements.identity_note: Rowe 2005 describes Siar-Lak as spoken on Lambom Island (data gathered during stays on Lambom), southern New Ireland; she reports no dialect variation among Lambom, Lamassa and Bakok, minor variation near the former Siar village on the east coast, and some variation at the northern end of the language area (which Lambom speakers regard as a Ramoaaina/Siar mixture). The stress statement is given for the language as a whole.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.recode_to: Keep classification fixed-dominant final (final stress). Replace the Wikipedia citation with Frowein 2011 §2.4 p.52 (primary) + Rowe 2005 §2.4 p.10; optionally add secondary-stress rhythm per Frowein (iambic right-to-left: 201, 0201, 20201), note no weight/length sensitivity (p.40), and lexical exceptions limited to Tok Pisin loans and a few proper nouns (dominant, not strict, is right).
audit.deciding_source_kind: database or survey citing another work
audit.reasoning: The record's classification (final fixed stress, dominant not strict) had no primary source: it quoted Wikipedia. I downloaded both primary descriptions from open repositories (Rowe 2005 via Internet Archive copy of the SIL PDF; Frowein 2011 via La Trobe OPAL figshare) and read the stress sections. Rowe p.10 states final stress verbatim as Wikipedia paraphrases; Frowein pp.52-55 confirms 'primary stress always falls on the final syllable' and adds secondary stress on alternate syllables leftward, loan/proper-noun exceptions, and no stress-length correlation (p.40). Nothing contradicts the classification; the fix is to re-cite to Frowein 2011/Rowe 2005 and upgrade the strength of the evidence (optionally encode secondary stress). No instrumental study exists per web search; Ross 2002 sketch is the only unheld description and is low priority.

sources.quote: Stress falls on the final syllable, and words have iambic feet. However, unstressed vowels are almost equal in length to stressed vowels unless a word has four or more syllables.
sources.locator: Ross, 'Siar', in Lynch, Ross & Crowley 2002, The Oceanic Languages (Routledge), section 1.2 Phonotactics and stress, printed p. 412
sources.note: Primary stress final; 'iambic feet' (plural) implies alternating secondary stress leftward, matching the catalog's fixed alternating stress from the right (Rowe 2005 p. 10), but the sketch gives no explicit secondary-stress rule or examples of it. Weight: not stated; syllables (C)V(C), closed syllables mostly word-final. Domain: word. Exceptions: none stated. Stress placement is used as a diagnostic for vowel+glide vs two-vowel sequences (/yay/ yai 'tree' vs /fa'in/ fain 'woman', p. 412).
